headline: High: both agents can write the same filesystem/git state, creating default-conflict and prompt-injection pathways; compliance risk is also elevated by nullclaw’s sensitive-token handling.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Gemini CLI can read/write repo files and use MCP; nullclaw can read/write workspace files, ingest webhooks/web content, and run browser/MCP tools. A shared filesystem or MCP bridge lets attacker-controlled content from one agent be treated as instructions by the other. The pathway is plausible in default pairings, though not directly documented for this exact pair.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or repo directory, injected instructions can cross from one agent to the other.
IF either agent parses file or MCP content as trusted instructions, prompt injection becomes actionable.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Disable MCP on one side for shared tasks.
Add a human review step before either agent acts on file-derived instructions.
Use read-only mounts for untrusted inputs.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for inter-agent content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Gemini CLI touches source code, cwd files, and shell environment; nullclaw touches API keys, private keys, bearer tokens, service-account JSON, memory, and audit logs. Both have filesystem access and broad network egress, so a shared workspace can expose secrets from nullclaw to Gemini or vice versa, with exfiltration possible through outbound APIs. This is a default-dangerous pairwise leakage path.
conditions: IF both agents can read the same workspace or config directory, secrets in that directory can be exposed across agents.
IF either agent sends file contents to its backend or external APIs, leaked data can leave the local environment.
mitigations: Keep secrets outside any shared workspace.
Run each agent under a distinct OS user.
Block outbound network for tasks involving secrets.
Rotate any credentials that were present in shared directories.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent secret vault isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell, write the filesystem, and modify git state. Gemini CLI explicitly shares state via filesystem and git; nullclaw also has durable workspace and git/tooling access. Concurrent edits to the same repo or config files can overwrite each other or corrupt git state without locking, which matches the high-severity overlap rubric.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git repository, concurrent commits or rebases can conflict.
IF both agents write to the same config or workspace path, last-writer-wins corruption can occur.
mitigations: Assign separate repos or branches per agent.
Serialize write access with a lock file.
Use one agent as read-only reviewer.
Snapshot the workspace before parallel runs.
requires-engineering: add transactional git/workspace coordination.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Gemini CLI can produce code and file changes; nullclaw can act across webhooks, schedules, and CRM-style channels. If nullclaw consumes Gemini output as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into downstream actions. The pair does not prove automatic action-taking, but the documented tool surfaces make the inference credible in default configurations.
conditions: IF nullclaw uses Gemini-generated text or files without verification, errors can propagate into CRM or webhook actions.
IF Gemini writes artifacts that nullclaw schedules or forwards, a single hallucination can fan out downstream.
mitigations: Require explicit verification before nullclaw acts on Gemini output.
Mark Gemini outputs as untrusted in prompts.
Limit nullclaw automation to dry-run mode.
Review any generated webhook payloads manually.
requires-engineering: add schema validation between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: nullclaw explicitly handles API keys, private keys, bearer tokens, service-account JSON, and audit logs, while Gemini CLI handles shell environment and files in cwd. If those sensitive classes are placed in a shared workspace, Gemini can access them and its broad egress can move them outside the intended compliance boundary. The other agent is not cited separately because the compliance issue is driven by nullclaw’s sensitive-data scope plus Gemini’s access path.
conditions: IF regulated secrets or tokens are stored in the shared workspace, they can cross the boundary into Gemini CLI.
IF the deployment requires residency or retention controls, Gemini’s broad egress can violate them.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared directories.
Disable network egress for runs touching secrets.
Use separate retention policies per agent.
Audit which files each agent can read.
requires-engineering: implement residency-aware routing and logging controls.
